input:
Case

This proposal concerns the company's vehicle fleet, which carries all of the company's delivery and service work and which currently runs entirely on diesel bought at retail prices. Fuel represents the largest single running cost, and it is a cost whose price is set entirely outside the company's control. At the same time, maintenance costs tend to rise as the fleet ages, and the oldest vehicles are the ones that spend the most time off the road. It is important to appreciate that replacement is already due for part of the fleet on age grounds alone, which means that the real choice is not between spending money and not spending money. The choice is between diesel replacements and electric replacements at a renewal point that will be reached in either case.

Electric vehicles are well suited to the greater part of the work the fleet carries out. Most routes are planned in advance, return to the depot each night, and sit comfortably within the range of the vehicles now available on the market. Overnight parking at the depot provides a long and predictable window for charging, and charging at the depot avoids any dependence on public charging infrastructure away from base. A minority of duties, however, do not suit early replacement: long routes with no fixed pattern, duties involving heavy payloads carried over distance, and work that depends on rapid turnaround away from base. Those vehicles will remain diesel at this stage and will be reconsidered when their own replacements fall due.

Drivers and depot staff have been consulted about the shape of the proposed change. The concerns they raised centred on range on the longest days, charging discipline at the depot, and cover arrangements when a vehicle is held for repair. Each of these concerns is addressed by the phasing set out in the schedule section below: replacement begins with the duties that suit electric operation best, and diesel cover is retained while the electric fleet settles into service.

It is also worth emphasising that the depot sits at the centre of the whole proposal. Every vehicle returns there, every charge is taken there, and the electrical capacity of the site therefore sets the pace of the entire change. A fleet that had to charge away from base would carry a rather different cost structure and a different risk profile. The proposal is accordingly built on depot charging throughout, and those duties that cannot return to the depot at night are among the ones held back for later replacement.

Costs

The capital cost of the proposal is $1453k. This capital covers the electric vehicles themselves together with the charging installation at the depot, including the chargers, the electrical works that the chargers require, and the civil works for the charging bays. Vehicle purchase accounts for the larger part of the capital. The depot works are the element most exposed to what the detailed design eventually finds, both in the ground and in the capacity of the existing electrical intake.

Running costs will change in structure rather than simply in size. Electricity replaces diesel as the energy cost, and overnight charging draws power at the hours when the depot is otherwise idle. Maintenance on the electric vehicles is expected to fall, because the drivetrain contains fewer wearing parts and because braking energy recovery reduces brake wear. Tyres, bodywork and damage costs remain unchanged in kind. Set against these changes are costs that diesel operation does not carry at all: charger maintenance, charge-management services, and the eventual battery replacement on those vehicles that are kept longest in service.

The appraisal horizon is 7 years. Residual values at the end of that horizon are uncertain for both fleets, and the appraisal treats them cautiously rather than resting the case on a favourable residual assumption. Battery life is the largest open cost item. The appraisal makes no battery-replacement allowance within the horizon and instead records the exposure as a risk to be carried into the detailed design stage, where vehicle selection and warranty terms will be able to price it. Two price exposures effectively change places under the proposal: diesel price exposure, which the company cannot realistically hedge at its scale, is replaced by electricity price exposure on overnight charging, which is contracted and broadly predictable over the appraisal period. Insurance, driver training and depot supervision costs are carried as unchanged in kind, and the balance between the lower energy and maintenance costs on the one hand and the new charging costs on the other is settled at the design stage, when both sides carry firm prices. Driver and depot staff training is carried within existing operating budgets and does not form part of the capital cost.

Schedule

Work will start one quarter after approval. The first stage is the detailed design, during which the depot's electrical capacity is assessed, charger positions are fixed against the parking layout, and vehicle selection is matched duty by duty against the work that each vehicle actually does. The design also settles the phasing of the programme, so that the vehicles replaced first are those whose duties suit electric operation and whose diesel predecessors are due for renewal.

Procurement follows on from the design. Vehicles are ordered against the design's selection, and the depot works are let as a separate package, so that installation can proceed while the vehicles are being built. The depot works are completed before the first vehicles arrive. Chargers are installed and commissioned on empty bays, and the charge-management system is set up and tested before it is required to carry the fleet.

Introduction is phased. Drivers receive instruction on the vehicles and on the charging routine before their own vehicles are changed, and the depot routine changes with the first group rather than after the last one. Diesel vehicles released by each phase are withdrawn at that phase, and the retained diesel cover shrinks as the electric fleet grows. The exposed dependency in the schedule is the depot electrical works: a connection upgrade, if the design shows that one is required, sits on the critical path and is commissioned before vehicle deliveries are accepted.

Two risks sit on the schedule. The first is the connection upgrade, whose timing rests with the network operator; the design stage opens that discussion before any vehicle order depends on the outcome. The second is vehicle supply against the phased plan: because orders are placed phase by phase, a delay in one phase moves that phase's withdrawals without holding up the vehicles that have already been converted. Instruction capacity is a third constraint, and training is therefore scheduled alongside the first phase rather than ahead of it.

Decision requested

Approval is requested to proceed to detailed design. Construction is not being requested at this stage, and no vehicle orders will be placed under this approval. The purpose of the design stage is to convert the estimates contained in this proposal into firm prices: depot works priced against a surveyed site, vehicles priced against named duties, and the battery exposure priced through warranty terms rather than left as an open allowance.

The design will return to the same decision body with a fixed capital price for the depot works and the charging installation, a vehicle-by-vehicle replacement list showing the duty each vehicle serves, and a phased schedule with its dependencies priced. The construction decision will then be taken on the basis of those products, not on the basis of this proposal.

If the design stage is declined, the renewal will simply proceed as like-for-like diesel replacement, vehicle by vehicle, without a priced electric alternative ever having been developed. Approving the design stage commits the design cost only. Both the construction decision and the vehicle orders remain open until the design reports. When the construction decision does come, it will be taken against three tests: the depot works at a fixed price, a vehicle list that matches vehicles to duties without spare capacity the duties do not use, and a schedule whose critical path no longer rests on an unpriced connection upgrade.
